after: ## What functionalism is trying to explain
alt: Because every known society ranks people unequally, functionalists ask what inequality does for society, not whether it is fair. Below, Parsons’ view that schools select people for roles links to Davis and Moore, for whom the reward system finishes the job schools start.
caption: Functionalists ask what inequality does for society, not whether it is fair.

after: ## How to apply the theory to an example
alt: Two panels. An air traffic controller needs rare skills, carries responsibility for many lives and trains for a long time, so high pay and prestige attract and motivate able people. A role almost anyone could learn quickly can be filled with lower rewards.
caption: Higher rewards go where skills are rare and responsibility is high, according to Davis and Moore.

alt: Five criticisms, each with an example: low-paid roles such as nursing can be vital; pay may reflect bargaining power, as with MPs; there is no proof exceptional talent is needed, since ministers need no formal qualifications; the pool of talent may be larger; and the Prime Minister is paid far less than a major chief executive.
caption: Each criticism needs its own example.

alt: A chain: unequal access to education and training means able people never get the chance to compete, so talent is wasted rather than discovered. Two more points: training may not be a sacrifice needing large rewards, and stratification can create hostility and distrust between groups.
caption: For Tumin, stratification can waste talent instead of finding it.

alt: Four rows build a paragraph. Point: Davis and Moore’s claim about unequal rewards. Application: a hospital consultant’s long training. Analysis: why the reward matters for the health service. Evaluation: feminists note nurses and care workers are essential but low paid and mostly women.
caption: Point, application, analysis, then evaluation from a named perspective.
